explanation: The hallway camera gets its power through the hallway smart plug. At 23:00, R1 switches that plug off to save energy, which also shuts the camera down. If the home is in away mode, the camera recording that R2 started stops without notice, so the front door isn't watched overnight.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only turns off the hallway plug when home_mode is not away. Even better, move the camera to a power source that the energy-saving rule never switches off.

explanation: R3 locks the front door when the home switches to night mode. R4 unlocks the same door when it detects motion in the hallway between 22:00 and 06:00. Night mode and that time window will usually overlap, so any hallway movement at night (a resident walking by, a pet) can unlock the door right after night mode locked it. The door would then stay unlocked overnight.
repair: Give R4 an extra condition so it only unlocks when home_mode is not night, for example a dedicated 'guests leaving' mode. Another option is to replace the motion trigger with a deliberate action, such as an indoor unlock button. You could also have the door re-lock itself after a short delay if it is still unlocked during night mode.

explanation: R1 turns on the living room heater at 18:00, and nothing ever turns it off. As the heater warms the room past 26 °C, R2 turns on the fan and opens the window. The heater then keeps running while cold outdoor air comes in, so the two rules work against each other and waste energy. The room temperature may also keep rising and falling around 26 °C.
repair: Add an action to R2 that turns off heater_living when the temperature goes above 26 °C. Also add a condition to R1 so the heater only turns on when window_living.position == closed and temp_living is below a comfort setpoint, for example 22 °C. This stops the heater and the open window from running at the same time.

explanation: These two rules can set each other off. When the living room gets above 26 °C, R2 opens the window, and in the heating season that can let in enough cold air to bring the room below 19 °C. That turns on the heater through R4 while the window is still open. Neither rule ever turns the heater off or closes the window, so the heater keeps running until the room passes 26 °C again and R2 fires again. You end up heating the outdoors, wasting energy and swinging between too hot and too cold.
repair: Add the condition 'window_living.position == closed' to R4 and make R4 close the window before turning on the heater. Also add the condition 'heater_living.power == off' to R2, or make R2 turn the heater off when it opens the window. This way the heater never runs with the window open.

explanation: Both rules fire at exactly 18:00. When the home is in away mode, R1 turns the living room heater on while R5 turns it off. The heater's final state depends on which rule runs last. If R1 wins, an electric space heater could run in an empty house and keep warming the living room.
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1, so it only turns the heater on at 18:00 when someone is home. The two rules then can't both apply at the same time, and R5 will reliably keep the heater off in away mode.

explanation: At 10:00 on weekdays R1 starts the robot vacuum, often while nobody is home. The living room motion sensor picks up the moving vacuum, and that wrongly tells R2 someone is home, so R2 unlocks the entrance door. The house can end up unlocked while it's empty, which is a security risk.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only unlocks when vacuum.mode == docked. Better still, base R2 on confirmed presence (for example a phone geofence or an authenticated arrival) instead of PIR motion alone.

explanation: On weekdays at 10:00, R1 starts the robot vacuum, usually while everyone is out and the home is in away mode. The living room motion sensor picks up the moving vacuum, so R3 sees motion while the home is away and sounds the siren. The result is a false alarm every weekday that nobody was in the house to cause.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only sounds the siren when vacuum.mode == docked. A better option is to use a pet-immune motion sensor or a sensor zone that ignores the vacuum. Either way, the alarm stays armed and still covers the other sensors while the vacuum runs.

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door so people can get out when the kitchen smoke detector goes off. R2 locks the same door whenever the home switches to away mode, and it doesn't check for smoke. If the home switches to away mode during a smoke alarm (or right after one), R2 can re-lock the door that R1 unlocked for evacuation. Neither rule rules out the other's situation, so they can send opposite commands to the same lock.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only locks the door when smoke_kitchen == false. Then away mode can't re-lock the door during a smoke event. Keep the smoke detector and R1's evacuation unlock active.

explanation: R1 turns the central air handler off when the kitchen smoke detector goes off, which helps keep smoke from spreading. R4 turns the air handler back on at 08:00 and doesn't check for smoke. If smoke is still being detected at 08:00, or is detected around that time, R4 overrides R1's safety shutdown. The air handler could then spread smoke through the apartment.
repair: Add the condition smoke_kitchen == false to R4, so the air handler only turns on at 08:00 when no smoke is detected. Keep R1's smoke shutdown and door unlock exactly as they are.

explanation: Rule R1 switches off the office plug at 00:30, and the Wi-Fi router is plugged into it, so the router loses power too. Without Wi-Fi, the garden camera can't upload to the cloud. That undoes R2, which turns cloud upload on in night mode, and night mode is almost certainly active at 00:30. Doorbell notifications also stop overnight, so you lose security coverage without any warning.
repair: Plug the Wi-Fi router into an outlet that is always on, not the switched office smart plug. That way R1 still cuts standby power to the desk devices, but the camera upload and doorbell notifications keep working overnight.

explanation: The router is plugged into the office smart plug. At 00:30, R1 switches that plug off to save standby power, which also shuts down the router and Wi-Fi. The doorbell sends its notifications over Wi-Fi, so after 00:30 you won't get any doorbell alerts. That happens even when R3 has turned notifications on because the home is in away mode. The garden camera's cloud upload also stops.
repair: Plug the router into an always-on outlet that the office plug doesn't control. If that's not possible, add a condition to R1 so it only switches the plug off when home_mode is not away.

explanation: The aquarium heater and pump are plugged into the living room power strip. When R1 switches the strip off at night, the heater and pump both lose power. After that, R2 can still "turn on" the heater when the water drops below 24 C, but nothing happens because the strip has no power. The water can keep cooling all night with no filtering or oxygen, which can harm the fish.
repair: Plug the aquarium heater and pump into an always-on outlet, or a socket on the strip that is never switched, separate from the TV standby devices. Then R1 only cuts power to the entertainment devices. Until you can re-wire, add a condition to R1 so it only turns the strip off when aquarium_heater and aquarium_pump are not connected to it.

explanation: R5 turns the aquarium heater off when the home goes into night mode. R2 turns the same heater on whenever the water drops below 24 °C. Once the heater is off, the water cools and R2 switches it back on. If night mode is entered or re-sent again, R5 turns it off again. The heater keeps flipping on and off, and the fish may spend the night in water that is too cold.
repair: Add a condition to R5 so it only turns the heater off when water_temp >= 24 (or a small margin above, such as 25 °C). Also give R2 priority so the heater can always come back on to protect the fish. A better option is to have R5 lower the heater's setpoint at night (for example to 24 °C) rather than cutting power completely.

explanation: Water for the garden sprinklers runs through the main water valve. When you're away, R1 closes that valve. R2 still starts watering at 06:00 every day, but no water can reach the sprinklers. So the controller says it's watering while the garden stays dry, and nothing tells you about it.
repair: Keep R1's leak protection as it is. Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when valve_main.state == open (or home_mode != away). If it's skipped, send a notification so you know the garden wasn't watered. If the garden must be watered while you're away, put the irrigation line on its own supply with a separate leak-protected valve, so the main valve can stay closed.

explanation: R2 starts watering at 06:00, which raises soil moisture until R4 fires and stops it. R4 only turns off 'watering' and leaves 'flow' on. R2 also never checks moisture, so it waters soil that is already wet. In that case R4 may never fire, because it only fires when moisture rises above 60 %.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when soil_moisture <= 60, and make R4 turn off both irrigation.watering and irrigation.flow (optionally stop at a slightly higher level, e.g. 62 %, so it doesn't switch on and off around 60 %).

explanation: The two rules control different devices, so they never give opposite commands to the same device. The conflict comes through the light sensor they share. When strong sun pushes the living room above 800 lux, R1 closes the blinds. Closed blinds block daylight, so the reading can fall below 150 lux, and then R2 turns on the ceiling lights in the middle of a sunny day. Nothing in these rules opens the blinds again, so the room can stay with blinds closed and lights on. It could also loop the other way: if the lights alone push the reading above 800 lux, R1 fires again. That is less likely, because ceiling lights rarely get that bright.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only turns on the lights when the blinds are open or it is after sunset. Then darkness caused by R1 closing the blinds during the day will not switch the lights on. Optionally, also lower R1's closing level to a partly-open setting (if the blinds support it), or add a rule that reopens the blinds when the lux level drops back to normal.

explanation: At 07:30, R3 opens the living room blinds. On a sunny morning, opening them lets in daylight, so the room's brightness can go above 800 lux, which makes R1 close the blinds again. Both rules can run within minutes of each other and set the same blinds to opposite positions, so the blinds open and then shut almost straight away. R1 then makes the room darker, so R1 won't fire again until the light rises above 800 lux once more.
repair: Make R1's glare protection win. Add a condition to R3 so it only opens the blinds if the outdoor or window-side light level is below the glare threshold (800 lux). If you don't have an outdoor light sensor, you could instead have R3 open the blinds only partway on bright mornings.

explanation: At 20:00, R1 turns on the nursery humidifier, which raises the room's humidity. Once humidity goes above 55 %, R2 turns on the dehumidifier. Since nothing turns the humidifier off, both machines run against each other all night. That wastes energy and makes the nursery's humidity unstable.
repair: Give the humidifier a humidity limit: only run R1 while humidity_nursery < 50, and add a rule that turns humidifier_nursery off when humidity reaches 55 %. Add the condition 'humidifier_nursery.power == off' to R2 so the dehumidifier never runs while the humidifier is on.

explanation: Both rules control the nursery dehumidifier's power and work against each other. R2 turns it on whenever humidity goes above 55 %, and R5 turns it off at 20:00. If humidity is still high at 20:00, R5 switches the dehumidifier off, humidity rises again, and R2 turns it back on during the night. That means the loud unit can still run while the baby sleeps, or the two rules keep switching it on and off.
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs between 07:00 and 20:00, which keeps the night quiet as R5 intends. To still protect against mould, add a separate night rule that turns the dehumidifier on only if humidity goes above a higher limit, for example 65 %.

explanation: At night, R1 turns off the bedroom wall switch. The bedroom bulb is wired behind that switch, so this also cuts the bulb's power. When the wake-up alarm rings the next morning, R2 tries to turn the bulb on to 60 %. The bulb has no power, so it can't respond and the wake-up light never comes on.
repair: Change R2 to turn the bedroom wall switch on first (switch_bedroom.power := on), wait a few seconds for the bulb to start up, then fade the bulb to 60 %. Another option is to change R1 so it turns off the bulb itself (bulb_bedroom.power := off) and leaves the wall switch powered.

explanation: Both rules control the same living-room thermostat, and their times overlap. R1 sets heat at 23 °C at 18:00. R2 sets eco at 19 °C whenever someone arrives between 17:00 and 19:00, and 18:00 falls inside that window. Depending on when someone gets home, one rule cancels the other: arrive at 17:30 and R1 changes the eco setting to 23 °C at 18:00; arrive at 18:30 and R2 drops the heating back to 19 °C. If someone arrives right at 18:00, the result depends on which rule runs last.
repair: Make the two rules cover different times so they never overlap. For example, limit R2 to arrivals between 17:00 and 17:59, and give R1 the condition "only if R2 hasn't set eco since 17:00". Or the flatmates can agree on one evening setpoint and replace both rules with a single rule.

explanation: Each rule changes the room temperature in a way that can set off the other rule. Neither rule ever switches its device off. Once R3 starts the AC cooling, it keeps cooling and can drag the room below 20 °C, which fires R4 and turns the heating on. The AC is still cooling at that point, so the heating and the AC end up running against each other and wasting energy. The 20–24 °C gap between the two thresholds only prevents this if each device is switched off before the room reaches the other rule's threshold.
repair: Make each rule turn off the other device and add a stop point. R3 should set thermostat.mode := eco as well as setting the AC to cool. R4 should set ac_living.mode := off as well as setting the thermostat to heat. Then add stop rules in the 20–24 °C gap: set ac_living.mode := off when temp_living <= 22, and set thermostat.mode := eco when temp_living >= 22.

explanation: When the home is in away mode, R1 turns off the garage circuit breaker. The garage exhaust fan is on that circuit, so it has no power. If carbon monoxide is then detected, R2 tries to turn on the fan, but the fan can't run. This safety ventilation fails silently exactly when nobody is home to notice.
repair: Move the garage exhaust fan (and the CO safety path) to a circuit that stays on, or change R1 so it only cuts power to the EV charger (e.g. set ev_charger.charging := off) instead of the whole garage breaker. Another option is to add a step to R2 that switches breaker_garage.power back on before it turns on the fan.

explanation: R2 opens the garage door when carbon monoxide is found in the garage. R3 closes the same door when the home switches to away mode. Neither rule checks the other's situation, so both can fire together. For example, you leave with a car still running or charging, then set away mode. The door could close while CO is still present, trapping the gas inside the garage, or the two rules could keep fighting over the door.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only closes the garage door when co_garage == false. Make the CO-ventilation rule (R2) take priority, so the door stays open and the fan keeps running until CO clears.

explanation: The EV charger runs on the garage circuit. If the car is parked in the garage and charging (R4), and the home then switches to away mode (for example, you leave on foot or in another car), R1 turns off the garage breaker. That cuts power to the charger and stops the charge R4 started, without any warning. Neither rule mentions this link, so the car may not be charged when you need it.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only switches off the garage breaker when car_present == false (or when ev_charger.charging == off). You could also wire the EV charger to its own circuit that R1 doesn't control.

explanation: At noon the feeder puts out food, and the cat runs into the kitchen. That sets off the kitchen motion sensor. If the home is in away mode at that time, R2 reads the motion as an intruder and sounds the indoor siren. You'd get a false alarm every day you're out at noon, and the siren would also scare the cat.
repair: Don't use the kitchen motion sensor alone to trigger the alarm in away mode. Either switch to a pet-immune motion sensor (or turn on its pet-immunity setting), or add a condition to R2 so it only sounds the siren if a door or window contact also opens. Another option is to have R2 ignore kitchen motion for a few minutes after the feeder dispenses. The alarm stays fully active either way.

explanation: Every day at 12:00, R1 dispenses cat food. The cat then runs to the feeder, which sets off the kitchen motion sensor. That makes R3 start recording on the kitchen camera even though no person or intruder is there. You end up with a security recording and possibly an alert every day at noon that was caused by your own feeding rule, which wastes storage and makes real events easier to miss.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it doesn't start recording during a short window after feeding (for example 12:00–12:15). Another option is to use a pet-immune or person-detection motion setting for the kitchen sensor, so the camera stays fully active the rest of the time.

explanation: Both rules start from the same event: motion in the kitchen. R3 always turns kitchen camera recording on, and R6 turns it off when the home is in 'home' mode. So when the household is in home mode, kitchen motion makes both rules fire at once with opposite commands. Whichever runs last decides whether the camera records, which defeats either the privacy goal or the security goal.
repair: Add the condition home_mode != home to R3 so it only records when the home is not in home mode. The two rules then never fire together, and recording stays on for security when the home is away/unoccupied.

explanation: R1 is labelled as switching off the phone charger at 23:30, but the CPAP breathing machine is also plugged into that bedside plug. When R1 cuts the plug's power, the CPAP turns off too. That undoes R2, which is meant to keep the CPAP on during night mode, and it can leave the resident without breathing support while asleep. R2 can't fix this by itself: it only runs when night mode starts, and even if it runs again, the CPAP has no power while the plug is off.
repair: Plug the CPAP into a regular wall outlet or its own dedicated outlet that no automation can switch off, so only the phone charger stays on plug_bedside. Until that's done, change R1 so it never turns off plug_bedside while the CPAP is drawing power or while home_mode == night.

explanation: Both rules control the same entrance lock but set it to opposite states, and neither rule checks the other's situation. If the resident falls in the evening and the home then switches to night mode, R4 re-locks the door that R3 unlocked for paramedics. If both events happen close together, the final lock state depends on which rule runs last, so emergency access could be blocked.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only locks the door when fall_detected == false (no fall emergency is active). Give R3 priority, so that once a fall is detected the door stays unlocked until a caregiver clears the alert by hand.

explanation: On a summer morning, R2 opens the living room window at 10:00 and lets hot outdoor air in. The room warms up, and once it passes 27 C, R1 turns on the AC. The AC then cools the room while the window is still open, so it fights the hot air coming in. That wastes energy and the room may never cool down properly.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so the AC only cools when window_living.position == closed. If the room is above 27 C while the window is open, close the window first and then start the AC. Optionally, also add a condition to R2 so the window only opens when the outdoor temperature is lower than the indoor temperature.

explanation: At 14:00 the lawn sprinkler turns on, and its spray wets the rain sensor on the terrace. The sensor then reports rain, which makes R4 close the bedroom skylight even though it isn't raining. So every day the skylight closes without a real reason, which works against airing out the summer house.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only closes the skylight when sprinkler.watering == off. Ignore rain readings while the sprinkler runs and for a few minutes afterwards. Another option is to move the rain sensor out of the sprinkler's spray area. Either way, real rain will still close the skylight.

explanation: R2 and R6 set the same living room window to opposite positions: R2 opens it at 10:00, and R6 closes it when the AC switches to cooling. R2 does not check the AC first. If the AC is already cooling at 10:00, R2 opens the window and R6 does not close it again, because R6 only reacts when the AC switches to cooling, not while it keeps running. The AC then cools a room with an open window. If the AC switches to cooling around 10:00, the window may open and close right away. In summer the open window also lets hot air in, which makes the AC work harder.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only opens the window at 10:00 if ac_living.mode == off. You could also extend R6 so it closes the window any time the window is open while the AC is cooling, not only at the moment the AC switches on.

explanation: When night mode starts, R2 turns off the closet power strip. The NAS and the cooling fan are both plugged into that strip, so they lose power too. At 01:00, R1 tries to start the NAS backup, but the NAS has no power, so the backup fails or gets cut off. If the strip is ever powered while a backup runs, the backup heats the closet. The fan shares the same strip, so its cooling depends on the same switch.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only switches the strip off when nas.backup == idle, and wait until the backup has finished. Or move the NAS and cooling fan to an outlet that is always on, so R2 only cuts power to devices that don't matter. The fan must keep running whenever the NAS is on.

explanation: When the home goes into night mode, R2 turns off the closet power strip. The cooling fan is plugged into that strip, so it loses power too. If the closet then gets hotter than 35 C, R3 tries to turn the fan on, but the fan has no power and nothing cools the closet. The NAS on the same strip also shuts off, which could stop a backup that is running.
repair: Plug the cooling fan into an outlet that is always on, not the switched strip, so R3 can still cool the closet at night. Also add conditions to R2 so it only cuts the strip when temp_closet <= 35 and nas.backup == idle.

explanation: If your teenager gets home between 23:00 and 06:00, R1 unlocks the front door. That unlock then sets off R2, which locks the door again right away. The two rules give opposite commands to the same lock, so the teen may be locked out or the lock may switch back and forth.
repair: Decide which rule should win at night. One option: add a condition to R1 so it only runs outside 23:00-06:00 and the teen uses a key or code at night. Another option: change R2 so it waits a few minutes after an unlock and checks that the door is closed before relocking, which gives a late arrival time to get inside before the door locks again.

explanation: At 09:00, R1 closes the office's exterior shades. That blocks the winter sun that would otherwise warm the room, so the office cools down. Once it drops below 20 °C, R2 turns the radiator on. The result is that the radiator burns energy to replace free solar heat the shades just shut out, and R1 ends up causing R2 to run when it otherwise might not.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it fully closes the shades only when temp_office is at least 21 °C, or when it isn't heating season. Otherwise, tilt the slats to cut screen glare while still letting solar heat in. If R1 does close the shades in cold weather, R2 still turns on the heat, so the office stays comfortable.

explanation: R1 and R6 both run at exactly 09:00 every day and give the same office shades opposite commands: R1 closes them for screen work and R6 opens them for daylight. Neither rule has a condition that separates them, so whichever command arrives last wins, and the shades may also move back and forth. There's a side effect too: when the shades end up closed, they block winter sun, so the office loses solar heat and gets cooler.
repair: Make the two rules mutually exclusive by adding a condition. For example, run R6 (open, for daylight and solar heat) only when temp_office is below the comfort setpoint, and run R1 (close, for screen glare) only when temp_office is at or above it. Another option is to merge them into one 09:00 rule that picks open or closed from the temperature.

explanation: At 19:30 R2 starts the white-noise speaker in the nursery. The baby monitor's microphone hears the white noise, so the nursery sound level goes up. If it goes over 60 dB, R1 thinks the baby is crying and turns on the nursery lamp, even though the baby is quiet. The light could then disturb or wake the baby.
repair: Make R1 tell crying apart from white noise. For example, while white_noise.playing == on, raise R1's threshold above the white-noise level (e.g. 'noise_nursery > white-noise baseline + 10 dB'). Or use the baby monitor's built-in cry detection instead of raw dB. Keep the white noise and the baby monitor running.

explanation: If the TV comes on after 20:00, R3 turns on the soundbar. The soundbar is on the other side of a thin wall from the nursery, so its sound pushes up the level the baby monitor measures. Once that goes over 60 dB, R1 thinks the baby is crying and turns on the nursery lamp, which could wake a sleeping baby. TV noise could also hide real crying, because the monitor can't tell the two apart.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only fires when the soundbar is off, or raise its threshold while the soundbar is on (or require the high level to last a short time). Also have R3 set the soundbar to a limited volume after 20:00, or move the soundbar off the shared wall.

explanation: During a frost warning, R1 turns the heater on, and it keeps warming the greenhouse. When the temperature goes above 18 °C, R2 opens the roof vent. The vent then lets out the heated air while the heater keeps running. This wastes energy, and on a frosty night it can let cold air in and work against the frost protection. The two rules can end up fighting each other.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so the vent only opens when frost_warning == false and gh_heater.power == off. Alternatively, first turn the heater off once the temperature goes above a setpoint, such as 18 °C, and open the vent only at a higher temperature, such as 24 °C.

explanation: The greenhouse heater is plugged into the outdoor smart plug. At 22:00, R3 switches that plug off, which also cuts power to the heater. Frost warnings usually cover the night, so the heater that R1 turned on can lose power during a frost. If a warning arrives after 22:00, R1 has no effect because the heater has no power, and plants could freeze.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it runs only when frost_warning == false. When a frost warning is issued, also have R1 turn plug_outdoor on before it turns on gh_heater. Another option is to move the heater to its own outlet that R3 does not control.

explanation: The greenhouse heater is plugged into the outdoor smart plug. At 22:00, R3 turns that plug off to save electricity, which also turns off the heater. If R1 switched the heater on because of a frost warning, the heater loses power on a cold night, exactly when frost is most likely, and the plants are left unprotected. There is also a smaller problem: once the heater warms the greenhouse above 18 °C, R2 opens the roof vent and lets the heat out, so the two rules end up working against each other.
repair: Add the condition "only if frost_warning == false" to R3, so the outdoor plug never turns off while a frost warning is active. You could also move the heater to its own outlet that is not on a schedule. Separately, make R2 open the vent only when the heater is off, or raise R2's threshold above the heater's target temperature.

explanation: R1 turns the greenhouse heater on when there's a frost warning. R6 turns the same heater off at 22:00 every night, whether or not a frost warning is in effect. Frost warnings usually cover the night, so the heater can be switched off at 22:00 exactly when frost protection is needed. R1 only fires when the warning is first issued, so nothing turns the heater back on, and the plants could freeze.
repair: Add the condition frost_warning == false to R6, so the 22:00 shut-off is skipped while a frost warning is active. Optionally, also have R1 turn the heater back on whenever a frost warning is active and temp_gh falls below a safe threshold.

explanation: R3 locks the front door when the home switches to night mode. R4 unlocks the same door when it detects motion in the hallway between 22:00 and 06:00. Night mode and that time window will usually overlap, so any hallway movement at night (a resident walking by, a pet) can unlock the door right after night mode locked it. The door would then stay unlocked overnight.
repair: Give R4 an extra condition so it only unlocks when home_mode is not night, for example a dedicated 'guests leaving' mode. Another option is to replace the motion trigger with a deliberate action, such as an indoor unlock button. You could also have the door re-lock itself after a short delay if it is still unlocked during night mode.

explanation: R1 turns on the living room heater at 18:00, and nothing ever turns it off. As the heater warms the room past 26 °C, R2 starts the ventilation fan and opens the window. The heater keeps running anyway, so heating and cooling run at the same time: energy is wasted, the room never settles at a steady temperature, and the window is left open with an electric heater on.
repair: Add a temperature limit to the heater: change R1 so it only turns the heater on if temp_living is below 22 °C, and add a rule that turns heater_living off when temp_living goes above 24 °C. That keeps the heater from ever pushing the room up to R2's 26 °C trigger. R2 should also turn heater_living off before it opens the window.

explanation: Both rules fire at exactly 18:00. When the home is in away mode, R1 has no condition, so it still turns the living room heater on while R5 turns it off. Which one wins depends on the order they run in, so the heater could be left running in an empty house.
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1, so it only turns the heater on at 18:00 when someone is home. The two rules then never apply at the same time.

explanation: At 10:00 on weekdays R1 starts the robot vacuum in the living room. A moving vacuum can set off the living room motion (PIR) sensor. R2 reads any motion there as "someone is home" and unlocks the entrance door. So the door could unlock during a weekday morning when the house is probably empty, which is a security risk.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only unlocks when vacuum.mode == docked. Better still, also require a confirmed resident presence signal, such as a phone geofence or a known person arriving. Motion alone should not count as proof that someone is home.

explanation: R1 starts the robot vacuum at 10:00 on weekdays, which is usually when nobody is home and the house is in away mode. The vacuum lives in the living room, and a moving vacuum can set off the living-room PIR motion sensor. That makes motion_living true, so R3 sounds the siren even though there's no intruder. The knowledge graph has no AFFECTS link from the vacuum to the motion sensor, so this conclusion relies on how PIR sensors usually behave, not on a stored fact.
repair: Change R3 so that while vacuum.mode == cleaning, living-room motion alone doesn't sound the siren. explanation: R5 and R2 give the aquarium heater opposite commands, and nothing stops them from firing at the same time. explanation: When you're away, R1 closes the main water shut-off valve. At 06:00, R2 still turns on the garden irrigation. explanation: R2 turns the sprinkler's watering on at 06:00 without checking the soil, and R4 turns the same watering state off once soil moisture is above 60 %. explanation: On a bright day, R1 closes the living room blinds to cut glare. explanation: These two rules send opposite commands to the living room blinds: R3 opens them at 07:30 and R1 closes them whenever it's brighter than 800 lux. On a sunny morning, R3 opens the blinds, sunlight pushes the brightness past 800 lux, and R1 closes them again right away, which undoes R3. The blinds may also flap open and closed if the brightness hovers around the 800 lux threshold.

Also give R1 a margin and a delay: for example, close only after the brightness has stayed above 800 lux for 10 minutes, and don't let R1 act within 30 minutes of R3 running.

explanation: R1 turns on the nursery humidifier at 20:00, and nothing ever turns it off. As it runs, it pushes the nursery humidity up. Once humidity goes over 55 %, R2 turns on the dehumidifier. The two machines then run against each other all night: they waste energy, make noise in the baby's room and keep the humidity swinging around the threshold.

Extend R2 so that when humidity goes over 55 %, it first turns the humidifier off and only turns on the dehumidifier if humidity is still above 55 % after a delay (for example, 30 minutes).

explanation: R2 and R5 send opposite commands to the nursery dehumidifier, and nothing stops them from overlapping. If the nursery is above 55 % humidity at 20:00, R5 turns the dehumidifier off. As soon as the humidity reading changes and is still above 55 %, R2 turns it back on. The dehumidifier then switches back and forth overnight. Either it runs loudly during sleep, or the room stays damp, which is the mould risk R2 is meant to prevent.

For nighttime, add a separate rule that turns the dehumidifier on only if humidity goes above a higher limit, for example 65 %, and preferably in a quiet or low-fan mode. That way mould protection still works at night without overriding R5 every time the humidity changes.

explanation: In this flat, the bedroom smart bulb gets its power through the smart wall switch. At night, R1 turns that switch off, so the bulb has no power. When the morning alarm rings, R2 tells the bulb to fade in to 60%, but nothing turns the switch back on first, so the bulb can't receive the command and stays dark.

Another option is to have R2 first set switch_bedroom.power := on, wait a few seconds for the bulb to start up, and then fade the bulb in to 60%.

explanation: Both rules control the same thermostat in the same time window and set it differently. At 18:00, R1 sets heat mode at 23 °C. If someone arrives home between 17:00 and 19:00, R2 sets eco mode at 19 °C. So the final setting depends on which rule fires last. For example, an arrival at 18:30 cancels R1's 23 °C, and an arrival at 17:30 is overridden at 18:00.

explanation: When you're away, R1 turns off the garage circuit breaker. The exhaust fan and garage door opener are garage devices and most likely run on that circuit. If carbon monoxide is then detected (for example, from an EV charger fault or a car left running), R2 tries to start the fan and open the door, but they may have no power. The CO safety response would then fail silently. The knowledge graph has no explicit power-dependency link, so this rests on the likely wiring, but the safety risk is high.

explanation: R2 opens the garage door when carbon monoxide is found in the garage. R3 closes the same door when the home switches to away mode. Neither rule checks the other's situation, so both can fire together. For example, you leave with a car still running or charging, then set away mode. The door could close while CO is still present, trapping the gas inside the garage, or the two rules could keep fighting over the door.

explanation: The wall-box EV charger is in the garage, and the smart breaker controls the garage circuit, so the charger almost certainly runs on that circuit. If the car is parked in the garage and the home then switches to away mode (for example, when you go on holiday and leave the car at home), R1 turns off the breaker. explanation: At 12:00 the feeder in the kitchen gives the cat food (R1). The feeder runs every day, including when you are away. The cat will likely come to the kitchen to eat. explanation: Both rules start from the same event: motion in the kitchen. R3 always turns kitchen camera recording on, and R6 turns it off when the home is in 'home' mode. So when the household is in home mode, kitchen motion makes both rules fire at once with opposite commands. explanation: Both rules control the same entrance lock but set it to opposite states, and neither rule checks the other's situation. explanation: The two rules control different devices, but they work against each other. At 10:00, R2 opens the living room window, which lets in warm summer air and can push the room above 27 °C. That makes R1 turn on the AC. The window stays open because no rule closes it, so the AC ends up cooling a room that is open to outside air. It wastes energy and may never get the room below 27 °C. explanation: R3 turns on the lawn sprinkler at 14:00. The sprinkler is next to the terrace, where the rain sensor is mounted. Spray from the sprinkler could wet the sensor and make it report rain, so R4 would close the bedroom skylight on a dry afternoon. This conflict comes from where the devices sit. The knowledge graph has no recorded physical link between them.

explanation: Both rules control the living room window, but they move it in opposite directions. R6 closes the window when the AC starts cooling. R2 opens it at 10:00 every day, even if the AC is already running. If the AC is cooling at 10:00, the window opens and stays open, because R6 only reacts when cooling starts. The AC then cools a room with an open window, which wastes energy and defeats the purpose of R6. If both rules fire at the same moment, whichever runs last decides the window's final position.

explanation: The NAS sits in the same closet as the smart power strip, so it is most likely plugged into that strip. Night mode usually starts before 01:00. If it does, R2 cuts power to the strip and the NAS shuts down, and the 01:00 backup from R1 can't run. If night mode starts while a backup is running, cutting the power could also corrupt the backup. explanation: If your teenager gets home between 23:00 and 06:00, R1 unlocks the front door. That unlock then sets off R2, which locks the door again right away. The two rules give opposite commands to the same lock, so the teen may be locked out or the lock may switch back and forth.

Another option: change R2 so it waits a few minutes after an unlock and checks that the door is closed before relocking, which gives a late arrival time to get inside before the door locks again.

explanation: At 9:00, R1 closes the exterior shades. That shuts out the morning sun, which would otherwise warm the office. Without that solar heat, the office can drop below 20 °C, so R2 turns on the radiator to replace warmth the sun would have provided for free. The two rules don't directly contradict each other, but R1 indirectly triggers R2, wasting energy. The knowledge graph has no AFFECTS link from shades to temperature, so this link is inferred from how exterior shades work and from the home's description.

That way glare protection doesn't block the free solar heat and force the radiator on. R2 stays as it is, so the room can still be heated when needed.

explanation: Both rules run at exactly 09:00 and control the same office shades. R1 closes them for screen work and R6 opens them for daylight. Neither rule has a condition that separates them, so the shades end up open or closed depending on which rule runs last, and they may move back and forth.

For example, close the shades if screen work is active or the sun on the office is strong (to limit glare and heat), and open them otherwise. explanation: R2 starts the white-noise speaker in the nursery at 19:30, and the speaker makes sound in the same room the baby monitor is measuring. If the white noise is loud enough at the monitor to go over 60 dB, R1 will take it for crying and turn on the nursery lamp for no reason, which could wake the baby. Also place the monitor away from the speaker or keep the speaker volume well under the limit. Keep cry detection switched on.

explanation: R1 turns the greenhouse heater on whenever there's a frost warning, and nothing caps its temperature. The heater warms the greenhouse air, which can push it above 18 °C and set off R2, so the roof vent opens during a frost. Cold air then comes in, the heater wastes energy fighting the open vent, and the plants may be exposed to frost.

explanation: When a frost warning comes in, R1 turns on the greenhouse heater, and nothing in the rules ever turns it off again. As the heater warms the greenhouse past 18 °C, R2 opens the roof vent, letting warm air out into freezing weather. The heater then keeps running against an open vent, which wastes energy and can let the plants get cold. R3 is not involved: nothing in the home's data says the heater or vent runs from the outdoor plug.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so the vent only opens when frost_warning == false and the heater is off (or raise its threshold while the heater is running). Also have the heater switch off once temp_gh reaches a set point, e.g. 16 °C, so it stops heating before the vent opens.

explanation: R1 turns the greenhouse heater on when there's a frost warning. R6 turns it off at 22:00 every night, and nothing stops it from doing that while a frost warning is still active. Frost warnings usually cover the night, so the heater would switch off just when the plants need it most. Because R1 only reacts when a warning is first issued, it won't turn the heater back on afterwards.
repair: Add a condition to R6 so it only turns the heater off at 22:00 if there is no active frost warning (frost_warning == false).

explanation: If the hallway camera is plugged into the hallway smart plug, R1 cuts its power every night at 23:00. R2 then can't record, even when the home is in away mode, which is when recording matters most. The camera fails silently, so you could lose security footage without knowing it. If the camera has its own power supply, there is no conflict.

explanation: R3 locks the front door when the home goes into night mode. R4 unlocks the same door whenever someone moves in the hallway between 22:00 and 06:00, which is the usual night-mode window. So after the door locks for the night, any hallway motion, even a resident walking to the bathroom, unlocks it again and leaves the apartment unsecured overnight. The two rules give opposite commands to the same lock at overlapping times.

Better still, don't use motion to unlock: let guests open the door from inside with the manual handle, or use a manual 'let guest out' button that locks the door again after a short delay.

explanation: R1 turns on the living room heater at 18:00, and nothing ever turns it off. As the heater warms the room past 26 °C, R2 fires and opens the window and turns on the fan. The heater keeps running the whole time, so the house heats air that goes straight out the window. That wastes energy, and the two rules keep working against each other.
repair: Add heater_living.power := off to R2's actions, so the heater stops before the window opens and the fan starts. Alternatively, give R1 a condition that only lets it run when the window is closed and the temperature is below a set comfort level, for example 22 °C.

explanation: Both rules run at exactly 18:00. R1 has no condition, so when the home is in away mode both rules fire together. R1 turns the living room heater on and R5 turns it off, so the result depends on which rule runs last. The heater could end up running in an empty house, or flip on and off.
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1, so the heater only turns on at 18:00 when someone is home. This makes the two rules mutually exclusive, and R5 keeps handling the away case.

explanation: At 10:00 on weekdays, R1 starts the robot vacuum. Nobody is likely to be home then. When the vacuum moves through the living room, the motion sensor can detect it as a person. R2 reads that motion as "someone is home" and unlocks the front door, which could leave the house unlocked while it's empty.
repair: Add conditions to R2 so it only unlocks the door when vacuum.mode != cleaning AND a real occupant is detected (for example, a resident's phone is home by geofence). Better still, don't use living-room motion as a reason to unlock the door at all.

explanation: R1 starts the robot vacuum at 10:00 on weekdays, which is usually when nobody is home and the house is in away mode. As the vacuum moves through the living room, the motion sensor can pick it up. R3 would then treat this as an intruder and sound the siren, so you could get a false alarm almost every weekday.
repair: Keep the alarm working, but add a condition to R3 so it only fires when vacuum.mode != cleaning (or ignore living-room motion while the vacuum is running and for a short time after it docks). Another option is to use a pet-immune motion sensor or keep the vacuum out of the motion sensor's area.

explanation: At 10:00 on weekdays, R1 starts the robot vacuum, which moves through the house. If it cleans the bedroom, the bedroom motion sensor can mistake it for a person. That would set off R4 and turn on the entrance light when nobody is there. The two rules don't give opposite commands. The problem is that the vacuum's movement changes the motion reading that R4 depends on.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only fires when vacuum.mode != cleaning, or require that someone is home. Another option is to keep the vacuum out of the bedroom, or away from the sensor's view, while R1's cleaning runs.

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door when smoke is detected so people can get out, and R2 locks the same door whenever the home switches to away mode. Neither rule checks the other's situation. If away mode turns on while smoke is still present (for example, the household leaves during the alarm and a geofence switches the mode), R2 locks the door again. That can block anyone still inside or slow down firefighters. It works the other way too: if smoke starts while the home is in away mode, R1 unlocks the door of an empty apartment.
repair: Add the condition smoke_kitchen == False to R2, so the door is not locked while smoke is present. Optionally, also send a notification when R1 unlocks the door while home_mode == away. Keep the smoke detector and R1's unlock-on-smoke behavior active.

explanation: When smoke is detected, R1 turns the air handler off so it doesn't spread smoke through the apartment. R4 turns the air handler back on at 08:00 no matter what. If smoke is still present at 08:00, for example during breakfast cooking, R4 undoes R1's safety shutdown and the air handler could spread smoke while people are evacuating.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only runs when smoke_kitchen == False. If smoke is present at 08:00, delay turning the air handler on until the smoke has cleared and the alarm has been reset.

explanation: These two rules can conflict. The home is described as a 'network dependency chain', which suggests the office plug powers the network equipment, such as the router or modem. At 00:30, R1 turns that plug off. That would cut the internet connection the garden camera needs for the cloud upload R2 turns on in night mode. explanation: R1 turns the office plug off every night at 00:30. The home's name ("network dependency chain") suggests this plug powers the network equipment (router or modem), though neither rule says so. If it does, the home goes offline, so the doorbell notifications that R3 turns on in away mode can't reach you. You would get no doorbell alerts after 00:30 while you're away. If the plug doesn't power anything the doorbell needs, there is no conflict.
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1 so the office plug stays on while you're away. Better still, move the router and modem to an always-on outlet so R1 only cuts power to true standby devices. Doorbell notifications stay on either way.

explanation: This is likely a conflict, but it depends on one thing the rules don't say: whether the aquarium heater is plugged into the living room power strip. Another option is a condition on R1: only turn off strip_living if it doesn't power the aquarium heater. If it does, switch off only the standby devices on their own outlets instead of the whole strip.

explanation: Both rules control the aquarium heater's power, and they give opposite commands. In night mode, R5 turns the heater off. The water then cools, and once it drops below 24 °C, R2 turns the heater back on. If night mode is set again, or the water is already cold when night mode starts, the heater can flip on and off, or stay off while the fish get too cold. The heater keeps the fish alive, so this is a real risk.
repair: Give the water temperature priority. Add a condition to R5 so it only turns the heater off at night when water_temp >= 25 °C. R2 should still always turn the heater on below 24 °C, even in night mode.

explanation: R1 closes the main water valve when the home goes into away mode. R2 starts watering every day at 06:00 with no conditions. The garden won't be watered even though the system reports watering as on, and a pump could run dry. Opening the valve to allow watering would remove leak protection while you're away.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when valve_main.state == open (or home_mode != away), and send a notification when watering is skipped. Leave R1's leak protection unchanged. If you need watering while away, put the irrigation on its own valve that R1 doesn't close.

explanation: R2 turns watering on at 06:00 every day without checking the soil, and R4 turns it off when soil moisture is above 60 %. If the soil is already wet at 06:00, the two rules give opposite commands to irrigation.watering. R4 may also never fire, because it reacts to moisture crossing 60 % and the soil is already past that point, so the garden could be watered when it's already wet. R4 also only switches off irrigation.watering and leaves irrigation.flow on. In a home set up for leak protection, that means water can keep running.
repair: Add the condition soil_moisture <= 60 to R2 so it only starts watering when the soil is dry. Also have R4 set irrigation.flow := off along with irrigation.watering := off.

explanation: Your garden irrigation most likely gets its water through the outdoor tap valve, though neither rule says so. When the house is in away mode, R5 closes that valve. R2 then still turns watering and flow on at 06:00 every day. The watering won't actually happen, and the controller or pump may run against a closed or dry line.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when valve_garden.state == open (or home_mode != away). Keep R5's leak protection as it is. If the garden needs watering while you're away, give the irrigation line its own supervised valve that opens only while watering is running.

explanation: On a bright day, R1 closes the living room blinds to cut glare. Sunlight gets swapped for electric light, which wastes energy and works against the point of using daylight. The two rules control different devices, so they never give opposite commands. repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only turns on the lights when the blinds are open or it is after sunset (blinds_living.position != closed OR sun below horizon). Another option is to have R1 tilt or partly close the blinds instead of closing them fully, so enough daylight stays above 150 lux.

explanation: At 07:30, R3 opens the living room blinds and lets daylight in. On a bright morning this can push the living room above 800 lux, which fires R1 and closes the blinds again. So the morning opening can be undone within minutes. Neither rule checks what the other one did.
repair: Add a condition to R3: only open the blinds at 07:30 if lux_living is 800 or less. Another option is to have R3 open the blinds partway (for example 50%) instead of fully, and to give R1 a hysteresis/delay (for example, lux > 800 sustained for 10 minutes) so a short burst of morning light doesn't close the blinds right away.

explanation: At 20:00, R1 turns on the nursery humidifier, which raises the humidity in the room. When humidity goes above 55 %, R2 turns on the dehumidifier in the same room. Neither rule turns its device off, so both machines can end up running against each other all night. This wastes energy and makes the nursery humidity swing up and down instead of staying steady.
repair: Give the humidifier an upper limit: add a rule that turns humidifier_nursery off when humidity_nursery reaches about 50 %. Then add the condition humidifier_nursery.power == off to R2, so R2 also turns the humidifier off before starting the dehumidifier. This way the two devices never run at the same time.

explanation: Both rules control the nursery dehumidifier's power, and they set it to opposite states. R5 turns it off at 20:00 so the baby can sleep. But R2 has no time limit, so whenever nursery humidity goes above 55 % during the night, R2 turns the dehumidifier back on. That undoes R5. If humidity is already high at 20:00, the dehumidifier may also switch off and then straight back on.
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs during the day (e.g., time between 07:00 and 20:00). For mould prevention at night, use a quiet or low-fan night mode, or briefly ventilate the room before 20:00.

explanation: The bedroom smart bulb gets its power through the bedroom wall switch. When night mode starts, R1 turns that switch off, which cuts power to the bulb. When the alarm rings the next morning, R2 tries to fade the bulb in to 60%, but nothing in the rules turns the switch back on first. The bulb has no power and can't respond, so the wake-up light never comes on.
repair: Make R2 turn switch_bedroom.power on first, then wait a few seconds for the bulb to start up before setting it to on at 60%. Another option is to change R1 so it turns off bulb_bedroom itself and leaves the wall switch powered.

explanation: Both rules control the same thermostat and their times overlap. R1 sets it to 23 °C in heat mode at 18:00. R2 sets it to 19 °C in eco mode whenever someone arrives between 17:00 and 19:00. If someone gets home between 18:00 and 19:00, R2 undoes R1's setting. If someone arrives just before 18:00, R1 undoes theirs. Which setting you end up with depends only on timing, so the thermostat can switch back and forth.
repair: Make the time windows not overlap: change R2's window to 17:00–17:59 so it only runs before R1, or add a condition to R2 so it skips if R1 has already set heat mode to 23 °C. Alternatively, agree on one evening setpoint and keep only the rule that sets it.

explanation: R3 and R4 never fire at the same moment because their temperature triggers don't overlap, but neither rule ever switches its device off. The air conditioner can keep cooling until the room drops below 20 C, which fires R4 and turns heating on while the AC is still cooling. The AC and the heating then work against each other in the same room, wasting energy and making the temperature swing.
repair: Make each rule switch the other system off: when R3 sets ac_living to cool, also set thermostat.mode := off; when R4 sets the thermostat to heat, also set ac_living.mode := off. Optionally, add a rule that turns both off once temp_living is back between 20 and 24 C.

explanation: R1 turns off the garage circuit breaker whenever the home goes into away mode. That breaker most likely powers the garage exhaust fan and the garage door opener, and maybe the CO sensor too. If carbon monoxide builds up while you're away, R2 will still fire, but the fan and door have no power, so the garage won't be ventilated. Nothing in either rule mentions this power dependency, which makes it a hidden safety risk.
repair: Wire the exhaust fan, garage door opener and CO sensor to a circuit that is always on, separate from the switchable garage breaker. Then R1 only cuts power to things that aren't needed for safety, like the EV charger and outlets. If rewiring isn't possible right away, add this step at the start of R2: turn breaker_garage.power on first.

explanation: R2 opens the garage door to vent carbon monoxide, and R3 closes the same door when the home goes into away mode. Neither rule checks the other's situation, so both can fire at once. For example, CO might still be present when everyone leaves, or the home might already be in away mode when CO is detected. If R3 runs after R2, the door closes, CO stays trapped in the garage, and the safety ventilation fails.
repair: Add the condition co_garage == False to R3, so the door only closes in away mode when no CO is detected. Also give R2 priority so it reopens the door if CO is detected after the door has closed.

explanation: The EV charger in the garage is most likely powered by the garage circuit breaker, though neither rule says so. If the car is parked and charging when the home switches to away mode, R1 turns the breaker off. That cuts power to the charger and stops the charging R4 started. The rules don't show this link, so the car can be left uncharged without any warning.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so the garage breaker only turns off when ev_charger.charging is off or car_present is False. Another option is to move the EV charger to its own circuit that R1 doesn't control.

explanation: R1 dispenses cat food at 12:00 every day, including when you're out and the home is in away mode, which is exactly when an automatic feeder matters most. Food being dispensed brings the cat running to eat. If the feeder is in or near the kitchen, the kitchen motion sensor will probably detect the cat, and R2 will sound the siren even though there's no intruder. This means you could get a false alarm around noon on any day you're away.
repair: Use a pet-immune motion sensor in the kitchen, or add a condition to R2 that ignores kitchen motion for about 30 minutes after the feeder runs. A second option is to require a second sign of entry before the siren sounds, such as a door or window contact opening. Keep the alarm itself enabled.

explanation: At 12:00, R1 makes the feeder dispense food. The feeder's own movement, or the cat coming over to eat, can set off the kitchen motion sensor. That makes R3 start recording on the kitchen camera at about the same time every day because of an expected pet event, not an intruder. This fills storage with false security clips and can bury real alerts. This only happens if the feeder or the cat's eating spot is where the kitchen motion sensor can see it. The rules don't say where the feeder is, so I'm assuming it's in or near the kitchen.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it doesn't trigger from feeding. One option is to ignore kitchen motion from 11:55 to 12:30, or only record when nobody is home. Another is to use a pet-immune motion sensor, or person detection on the camera, so the cat doesn't trigger it. Keep the camera and motion sensor working as they do now.

explanation: Both rules start when the kitchen detects motion. If the home is in home mode, R3 turns the kitchen camera recording on and R6 turns it off at the same moment. Whether the camera ends up recording depends on which rule runs last, so you can't count on it either for privacy or for security.
repair: Add the condition home_mode != home to R3, so it only records when the home is not in home mode. The two rules then never fire together.

explanation: R3 unlocks the entrance door when a fall is detected so paramedics can get in. R4 locks the same door when the home goes into night mode. Neither rule has a condition that keeps it from firing at the same time as the other. A fall at night is a likely case for an elderly resident. If night mode turns on, or turns on again, after a fall, the door gets locked again and paramedics may not be able to get in.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only locks when fall_detected == False and no emergency is active. Also give R3 priority: keep the door unlocked until a caregiver or paramedic manually clears the fall alert.

explanation: These two rules conflict through the room's temperature. At 10:00 R2 opens the living room window, and in summer that lets warm outside air in. Once the room goes above 27 °C, R1 turns on the AC, which then cools a room with an open window. The AC wastes energy, may never cool the room enough, and keeps running. Nothing in either rule checks the state of the other device.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only cools when window_living is closed. Also add a condition to R2 so it only opens the window when ac_living is not cooling, or when the outside temperature is lower than temp_living.

explanation: R6 closes the living room window when the AC starts cooling. R2 opens the same window every day at 10:00 and checks nothing first. If the AC is already cooling at 10:00, R2 opens the window anyway. R6 won't close it again because it only reacts when cooling starts. The window then stays open while the AC runs, which wastes energy and works against what R6 is meant to do.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only opens the window when the AC is not cooling (ac_living.mode != cool).

explanation: In a server-closet home lab, the NAS is very likely plugged into the closet power strip. Night mode usually starts before 01:00. If it does, R2 cuts power to the strip, so the NAS is already off when R1 tries to start the backup at 01:00 and the backup fails. If night mode starts while a backup is running, R2 cuts power mid-backup, which can corrupt data. The rules never mention this power link, which is why this is a physical conflict.
repair: Plug the NAS (and any closet cooling) into an always-on outlet that R2 doesn't control. If that isn't possible, add a condition to R2 so it only turns off the strip when nas.backup is not running and the time is outside the backup window (for example, after the backup finishes).

explanation: R2 turns off the closet power strip every night. If the closet fan is plugged into that strip, the fan has no power at night. When the closet goes above 35 °C, R3 will still send 'fan on', but the fan won't run and the equipment in the closet may overheat. The rules don't say where the fan gets its power, but in a server closet setup it is likely the strip.
repair: Plug the closet fan into an outlet that is always on, not the switched closet strip. If that isn't possible, add a condition to R2 so it only turns off the strip while temp_closet is below about 30 °C. You could also have R3 turn strip_closet.power on before turning the fan on.

explanation: If the teenager gets home between 23:00 and 06:00, R1 unlocks the front door. That unlock is exactly what triggers R2, which locks the door again straight away. The two rules end up fighting over the same lock: the teen may be locked out right after the door 'opens' for them, and the lock could keep switching back and forth.
repair: Make the night rules explicit. Option 1: add the condition 'time not in [23:00, 06:00]' to R1, so the teen uses a key or code at night. Option 2: change R2 so it only re-locks after a delay (e.g., the door has stayed unlocked and closed for 2–5 minutes), so the teen can get in and the door is still locked again afterwards. Either way, the door ends up locked at night.

explanation: The two rules control different devices, but they're linked through the room temperature. At 09:00, R1 closes the office shades, which blocks the sun from warming the office. The room can then cool below 20 °C, so R2 turns on the radiator to replace heat the sun would have provided for free. This wastes energy, and the radiator may run on sunny mornings when it otherwise wouldn't need to.
repair: Give R1 a temperature check: close the shades fully only when temp_office is 21 °C or higher (or only when there's glare). Otherwise, tilt or partly close them so the sun can still warm the room. Another option is to have R2 skip heating while the shades were closed less than about 30 minutes ago and the outdoor sun is strong.

explanation: R1 and R6 both run at exactly 09:00 every day with no conditions, and they send opposite commands to the same office shades: R1 closes them and R6 opens them. Where the shades end up depends on which command happens to run last, so you can't predict it, and the shades may jump back and forth.
repair: Make the two rules mutually exclusive by adding a condition. For example, R6 opens the shades at 09:00 only when outdoor light or solar gain is low (e.g. outdoor illuminance below a threshold or cloudy). R1 closes them at 09:00 only when sunlight is strong (glare or heat gain on the screen). Another option is to merge both into one 09:00 rule that picks open or closed based on that light condition.

explanation: R2 starts the white-noise speaker in the nursery at 19:30. That adds sound to the same room where R1 listens for crying above 60 dB. If the white noise is loud enough, or adds to normal background sound so the level goes over 60 dB, R1 will think the baby is crying and turn on the lamp, which could wake the baby. The constant noise can also make it harder to tell real crying apart, so the 60 dB limit stops being a reliable sign that the baby is crying.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so that while white_noise.playing == on, the lamp only turns on when noise_nursery goes above a higher limit set from the measured white-noise level (for example, about 10 dB above it). Alternatively, use a cry-detection signal from the baby monitor instead of the raw sound level. Also keep the white-noise volume clearly below 60 dB at the sensor.

explanation: After 20:00, R3 turns on the soundbar whenever the TV turns on, and the extra sound can raise the noise level picked up in the nursery. R1 treats any nursery noise above 60 dB as a crying baby, so loud TV audio could turn on the nursery lamp falsely, at bedtime, and possibly wake the baby. How likely this is depends on how well sound travels from the TV room to the nursery, which the rules don't say.
repair: Make R1's cry detection stricter without turning it off: require noise_nursery > 60 dB for at least 10-15 seconds, and while the soundbar is on, only fire if the nursery reading is clearly louder than the TV-room level or the baby monitor's own cry detection confirms it. Optionally, cap the soundbar volume after 20:00.

explanation: During a frost warning, R1 turns the heater on. Nothing tells the heater when to stop, so it can warm the greenhouse past 18 °C, which triggers R2 and opens the roof vent. Freezing outside air then comes in while the heater keeps running. That wastes energy, can expose plants to cold drafts, and makes the two devices work against each other.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so the vent only opens when frost_warning == False and gh_heater.power == off. Also give R1 a temperature limit: turn the heater off when temp_gh reaches about 15 °C, which keeps it below the 18 °C vent threshold.

explanation: In a garden greenhouse the heater is often powered from the outdoor socket. If gh_heater is plugged into plug_outdoor, R3 cuts its power at 22:00 even after R1 has turned it on for a frost warning. Frost risk is highest at night, so the plants would lose heat when they need it most, and the heater would still show as 'on' in the system. If the heater is on a separate circuit, there is no conflict.
repair: Add the conditions 'frost_warning == False AND gh_heater.power == off' to R3 so the outdoor plug is never switched off while the heater needs power. Alternatively, move the heater onto a circuit that the 22:00 shut-off does not control.

explanation: During a frost warning, R1 turns the heater on with no stop condition, so the greenhouse can go above 18 °C. That triggers R2, which opens the roof vent and lets warm air escape into frosty air while the heater keeps running. This wastes energy, and if the vent stays open after the heater falls behind, the plants could get cold.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so the vent only opens when there's no frost warning (frost_warning == False). Better still, have the heater shut off at about 18 °C so it doesn't push the temperature high enough to open the vent.

explanation: R1 turns the greenhouse heater on when a frost warning comes in, and R6 turns it off at 22:00 every night no matter what. Frost warnings are usually for the night, so a warning issued in the evening can still be active at 22:00. In that case R6 switches the heater off right when the plants need it most. R1 only runs when a warning is first issued, so the heater stays off for the rest of the frosty night.
repair: Add a condition to R6 so it only turns the heater off at 22:00 if frost_warning == False. That way the heater keeps running through the night while a frost warning is active.
